title: 6. The open lakehouse
summary: Object storage plus Iceberg tables plus a shared catalog, so that many engines read and write one copy of governed data, organised as medallion layers with a semantic layer on gold.

blocks.text: 42.1 Context and the problem it solved

By the late 2010s many companies ran two platforms: a data lake on object storage for raw files, data science and cheap retention (chapter 38), and a cloud warehouse for curated, governed BI (chapters 37 and 41). Data was copied between them, so tables existed twice, with two security models and disagreements about which number was right.

The lake was cheap but unreliable: no transactions, no safe concurrent writes, no clean row updates or deletes. Open table formats (chapter 21) fixed that layer, so warehouse-style guarantees could live on the lake itself. The **open lakehouse** is the architecture that results: one copy of data in an open format, one catalog, many engines.
This chapter describes the **open** variant on **Apache Iceberg** with a **REST catalog**, where no single engine owns the data.

blocks.text: Read the stack bottom-up. Object storage holds immutable files; Iceberg metadata says which files make up each snapshot. The catalog stores the one thing that must be atomic: the pointer from a table name to its current metadata file, and a commit is a compare-and-swap on it (chapter 22). Engines resolve tables through the catalog, prune files with manifest statistics and read Parquet directly.

Every medallion layer (chapter 12) is an Iceberg table in the same catalog: Flink might write bronze, Spark builds silver and gold, Trino serves ad hoc queries and Snowflake reads gold for BI, with no copies.

blocks.text: Engine support for Iceberg is uneven and moves fast: some engines only read, some support only certain catalogs, and newer spec features (format v3) arrive at different times. Test the exact operations you need (MERGE, schema evolution, deletes, branches) against current documentation.
42.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

Bronze tables are append-only Iceberg tables partitioned by ingestion day, keeping source payloads close to their original shape plus load metadata. Silver tables are conformed entities maintained with `MERGE INTO`, often with copy-on-write for read-heavy tables and merge-on-read for tables receiving frequent small CDC updates (chapter 23). Gold holds dimensional marts or wide tables (chapters 8 and 11) shaped for the semantic layer.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: a silver table maintained from bronze CDC
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE lake.silver.customers (
  customer_id BIGINT,
  email STRING,
  country STRING,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP
) USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (bucket(16, customer_id))
TBLPROPERTIES ('write.merge.mode' = 'merge-on-read');

MERGE INTO lake.silver.customers t
USING (
  SELECT * FROM lake.bronze.customers_cdc
  WHERE _loaded_at > '2026-11-16 00:00:00'
) s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'd' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET email = s.email, country = s.country, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'd' THEN INSERT (customer_id, email, country, updated_at)
  VALUES (s.customer_id, s.email, s.country, s.updated_at);

The source batch must first be deduplicated to the latest change per key, or the MERGE fails on multiple matches. Physical design is yours: partition transforms, sort order and target file size (often 128-512 MB) decide pruning, since no warehouse optimiser reorganises data for you. Snapshots give time travel but are not a history model; keep SCD2 dimensions (chapter 9) and expire snapshots.

**Snowflake** fits in two ways (chapter 28): as a reader of externally catalogued Iceberg tables through a catalog integration, or as the owner of Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables that other engines read through a catalog. Write support for externally managed tables has been expanding; check the current documentation. The **semantic layer** sits on gold only: metrics defined on silver tend to duplicate business logic and break when silver is refactored (chapter 36).
42.5 Ingestion, orchestration and serving

items: **Ingestion:** CDC or events land in bronze through Flink or the Kafka Connect Iceberg sink, committing every 1-10 minutes; batch extracts through Spark. Commit interval drives small-file counts.

**Orchestration:** Airflow or Dagster runs transformations and, just as important, table maintenance: compaction (`rewrite_data_files`), snapshot expiry, orphan file removal and manifest rewrites (chapter 25). Lakehouses that skip maintenance degrade within weeks.
**Serving:** Trino or Snowflake for BI, DuckDB or Spark for notebooks, a semantic layer generating SQL. Sub-second user-facing analytics needs a serving store (chapter 46).

**Governance:** the catalog is the enforcement point. Credential vending lets the catalog hand engines short-lived, table-scoped storage credentials; row filters and masking are still largely enforced per engine (check your catalog's current capabilities).

blocks.text: Giving every engine direct read-write IAM access to the bucket bypasses the catalog entirely. Route all access through the catalog and keep raw bucket permissions for maintenance roles only.

Strength

blocks.text: 42.7 When to choose it, and when not

items: Choose it when several engines genuinely need the same data (Spark for ML, Snowflake for BI, Flink for streaming).
Choose it when avoiding format lock-in is a strategic requirement, not just a preference.
Choose it when you have, or will fund, a platform team that can operate catalogs, compaction and access control.
Avoid it when one warehouse serves all workloads well and the team is small; the modern data stack (chapter 41) is simpler.
Avoid it when the main need is sub-second user-facing queries; add an OLAP serving store instead (chapter 46).

blocks.title: Retailer consolidating a lake and a warehouse
blocks.text: A retailer kept 300 TB of clickstream in a Parquet lake and copied sales data into a warehouse nightly; finance and data science reported different revenue because the copy logic drifted. The team moved all layers to Iceberg in a REST catalog: Spark builds silver and gold, Snowflake reads gold through a catalog integration, data science reads silver from Spark and DuckDB.
items: Nightly copy removed; both groups read the same gold snapshot
Revenue metric defined once in the semantic layer on gold
Open issue: row-level security configured twice, in Snowflake and Trino

blocks.title: Design a lakehouse for three engines
blocks.text: You have 80 TB of order and event data. Data science uses Spark, analysts use Snowflake, and a fraud team wants Flink to write near-real-time features. Sketch the catalog, which engine writes which layer, the streaming commit interval, the maintenance schedule and how analysts are kept away from raw PII in bronze.
hints: Decide which engine is the single writer for each table
Think about where masking policies are enforced
Consider what happens to file counts with one-minute commits

items: The open lakehouse is object storage plus Iceberg plus a shared catalog, with interchangeable engines.
The catalog's atomic pointer swap is the commit; route all access through it.
Medallion layers are Iceberg tables; physical design and maintenance are yours.
Snowflake can be a reader or an owner of Iceberg tables; the semantic layer sits on gold.
The main costs are uneven engine support, maintenance and governance spread across engines.

blocks.q: What makes a commit to an Iceberg table atomic in an open lakehouse?
options: Parquet files are written in a single multipart upload
The catalog swaps the table's current metadata pointer with compare-and-swap
The orchestrator runs only one job at a time
Each engine locks the S3 prefix while writing
blocks.explain: Iceberg commits by atomically replacing the metadata pointer in the catalog. Object stores have no prefix locks, and single-file atomicity does not make a multi-file change atomic.

blocks.q: A lakehouse's queries have become slow and expensive after six months of one-minute streaming commits. What is the most likely cause?
options: Small files and accumulated snapshots because compaction and expiry were not scheduled
The catalog has too many namespaces
Parquet is a row format and cannot be pruned
Iceberg does not support streaming writes
blocks.explain: Frequent commits create many small files and snapshots; without compaction and expiry, planning and scanning cost grows. Iceberg supports streaming writes, and Parquet is columnar.

blocks.q: Where should the semantic layer's metric definitions be built in this architecture?
options: On bronze, to stay close to the source
On silver, because it is conformed
On gold tables shaped for consumption
blocks.explain: Gold is the stable consumption contract. Metrics on silver duplicate business logic and break on refactoring; per-tool definitions recreate inconsistency.

blocks.q: Which situation argues most strongly against adopting an open lakehouse?
options: Several engines that must read the same 200 TB of data
A requirement to avoid storage format lock-in
A five-person team whose BI needs are fully met by one cloud warehouse
Long retention requirements on large event data
blocks.explain: The lakehouse pays off with multiple engines, scale or openness requirements. A small team served by one warehouse would take on catalog and maintenance work for little benefit.
